topic: connecting numerical, graphical and algebraic ideas of a limit
subtitle: reading a limit from a table, from a graph, from algebra, and as the limit of partial sums

problems.note: Warm-up: read the limit off a completed two-sided table.
0/0 on substitution; factor the difference of squares and cancel.

traps.desc: read the indeterminate form 0/0 as the answer 0 instead of rewriting

problems.note: Graph is the line y = x + 2 with a hole at (2, 4): the limit exists even though the value does not.
Finite partial sum written in sigma notation.

traps.desc: stopped one term early, adding only the terms through n = 4

problems.note: Table entry the student computes, approaching 0 from the right.
Table entry approaching 0 from the left.
The exact limit the table is pointing at.

traps.desc: after rationalizing, reported the denominator sqrt(1)+1 instead of its reciprocal

problems.note: Difference of cubes over difference of squares; the common factor (x-2) cancels.

traps.desc: dropped the middle term and factored the cube as (x-2)(x^2+4), giving 8/4

problems.note: Left branch of the graphed piecewise function.
Right branch of the graphed piecewise function.

problems.desc: Explain why the two-sided limit at x = 1 does not exist: the one-sided limits are 2 and 3, and a two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and agree. Accept any answer making that comparison; do not accept 'because there is a break in the graph' with no reference to the two one-sided values.

problems.note: Infinite geometric series with a = 3, r = 1/2.

traps.desc: took the n = 1 term as the first term, using a = 3/2 in a/(1-r)

problems.note: Rationalize with the conjugate; confirms the numerical answer of problem 5's method.
End behaviour the table is pointing at.

traps.desc: divided the leading coefficients the wrong way round, reporting 1/2

problems.note: Graph flattens toward the horizontal asymptote y = 3.

traps.desc: read the y-intercept off the graph instead of the end behaviour, giving 1/2

problems.note: Synthesis: the sum of the infinite series.

traps.desc: used a = 1 in a/(1-r) instead of the actual first term a = 1/2

problems.desc: Explain how the three representations agree: the partial sums 1/2, 3/4, 7/8, 15/16, 31/32 climb toward 1 numerically, the graph of the partial sums flattens against the line y = 1, and the sum of an infinite series is DEFINED as the limit of its partial sums. Accept any answer that names the sum as a limit rather than an ordinary addition; do not accept 'you add up all the terms'.
